questions.question: Which description of encapsulation matches the two points in the lecture?
options: Creating many objects from one class so that data is copied safely
Splitting a class's data and its methods into two separate classes
A child class reusing the fields and methods of its parent
Keeping data and the behaviour that works on it together in one object (a capsule), and not giving unrestricted access to that data
questions.explanation: The notes define encapsulation as (1) data and behaviour kept together within an object and (2) no unrestricted access to the data, which in BankAccount means a `private` balance changed only through `deposit`/`withdraw`. Reusing a parent's members is inheritance, a different pillar.

questions.question: Which line fails to compile?
options: Line 1: a private field cannot be modified even inside its own class
Line 2: `deposit` takes an int but `balance` is a double
Line 3: `balance` is private, so code outside `BankAccount` cannot access it
Line 4: a public method cannot return a private field
questions.explanation: `private` restricts access to the declaring class only, so `Demo` cannot touch `ba.balance` directly; that is exactly the `ba.balance = 1,00,000 (X)` case in the notes. Methods of BankAccount itself (line 1, and the public getter) may freely read and write the private field, and an int added to a double is widened automatically.

questions.question: Which mapping of Java's four access modifiers is correct?
options: private: same class only; default (no keyword): same package; protected: same package + child classes; public: anyone
private: same package; default: same class only; protected: anyone; public: same package + child classes
private: same class only; default: anyone; protected: child classes only (not the package); public: same package
private: child classes; default: same package; protected: same class only; public: anyone
questions.explanation: As listed in the notes: private is class-only, default (no modifier) allows anyone in the same package, protected adds inherited (child) classes on top of the package, and public allows everyone. A common mistake is thinking protected excludes the package; it actually includes it.

questions.question: In the lecture's BankAccount, `withdraw` has the comment `// amount <= balance` but no check, so balances can go negative. How does encapsulation let you fix this for every caller?
options: Make `balance` public so callers can check it themselves before withdrawing
Add the check inside `withdraw` (e.g. reject when amount > balance); since `balance` is private, all changes must go through this method and cannot bypass it
Add a public setter `setBalance(double b)` with no checks so callers can correct negative values
Mark `withdraw` as private so nobody can call it
questions.explanation: Because `balance` is private, the only way to change it is through BankAccount's methods, so a validation inside `withdraw` (or a setter) protects every caller at once, just like the 'college should be real' validation comment in `setCollege`. Making the field public, or adding an unchecked setter, re-opens unrestricted access; a private withdraw makes the feature unusable.

questions.question: Based on Demo3 (parent Student, child EngineeringStudent), which marked line does not compile?
options: Line 1: `markAttendance` is defined in Student, not EngineeringStudent
Line 2: `attendLab` has default access and cannot be called from Demo3
Line 3: a parent object cannot call its own methods once it has a child class
Line 4: a plain `Student` object has no `attendLab` method; only the child class adds it
questions.explanation: Inheritance flows from parent to child: EngineeringStudent is-a Student, so it gets `markAttendance` plus its own `attendLab`. A Student is not an EngineeringStudent, so `s1.attendLab()` does not compile (marked '(wrong)' in Demo3). Default access is fine here because all classes are in the same package.

questions.question: The project has `college.Student` and `school.Student` (both public). A teammate writes `import college.*; import school.*;` and then `Student s = new Student();` in Demo2. What happens, and how does the lecture's Demo2 avoid it?
options: It compiles and uses `college.Student`, because that import comes first
It compiles and uses `school.Student`, because the last import wins
Compile error: `Student` is ambiguous; Demo2 uses fully qualified names like `new college.Student()` and `new school.Student()`
Compile error: two packages may never contain classes with the same name
questions.explanation: Both wildcard imports bring in a class named `Student`, so the simple name is ambiguous and the compiler refuses to pick one; import order does not matter. Packages exist precisely so that same-named classes can coexist, and Demo2 distinguishes them with the fully qualified `packageName.ClassName` form.

questions.question: Why does Java not allow `class D extends B, C`, according to the lecture?
options: Because of the diamond problem: if B and C both override A's `show()`, the call `d.show()` would be ambiguous
Because a class with two parents would need twice as much heap memory
Because `extends` can only be used once per package
Because multilevel inheritance (A -> B -> C) already gives exactly the same result
questions.explanation: With A at the top and B and C each providing their own `show()`, a D inheriting from both would not know which version `d.show()` should run; this is the diamond problem. Java supports single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance of classes, and the notes point to interfaces as the way around it. Multilevel inheritance is a different shape, not a substitute.

questions.question: Building on the notes' `class A { int x = 4; }` / `class B extends A { int x = 5; }` example, what does `new B().show();` print?
questions.explanation: Inside B, plain `x` is B's own field (5) and `super.x` is the parent's hidden field (4). B does not override `greet()`, so both `super.greet()` and `greet()` run A's method, and code in A that says `x` always refers to A's field, giving A4 twice. Fields are not overridden like methods, which is why 'A5' is wrong.

questions.question: Extending Demo5 with a multilevel class, what does `new CSEStudent().print();` print?
options: S0 S1 E C Aditya IIT G
C E S1 Aditya IIT G
S1 E C Aditya IIT G
S1 E C IIT G
questions.explanation: Each constructor first runs the parent constructor it names: CSEStudent -> EngineeringStudent(name, college) -> Student(name), so the prints come out top-down: S1, E, C. Because `super(name)` is called explicitly, the no-arg Student() never runs (no S0). CSEStudent inherits EngineeringStudent's `print()`, which calls `super.print()` first (Aditya) and then prints the college.

questions.question: In Demo5, a teammate deletes the empty `Student() {}` constructor (keeping `Student(String name, int age, int rollNo)`) and adds a new constructor `EngineeringStudent(String college) { this.college = college; }`. What happens?
options: It compiles; the new constructor simply leaves name, age and rollNo at their defaults
It compiles, but `new EngineeringStudent("IIT G")` throws an exception at run time
Compile error in the existing four-argument constructor, because it calls `super(...)` with arguments
Compile error in the new constructor: the compiler inserts an implicit `super()`, but Student no longer has a no-argument constructor
questions.explanation: A constructor that does not call `super(...)` or `this(...)` gets an implicit `super()` call to the parent's no-arg constructor. Once Student declares a parameterized constructor, no default one is generated, so removing `Student() {}` leaves nothing for `super()` to call: a compile-time error. The existing constructor is fine because it explicitly calls `super(name, age, rollNo)`.
